Note · AWS — Building Mechanisms & the Operational Readiness Review

6 min read1,391 wordsUpdated 2026-10-19notes/canon/canon-aws-mechanisms-orr.md

Canon · Cluster: Org Design & Mechanisms · Maps to E11 (Personal Operating System), E5 (Transformation), Course 06 (Operations), E1 (Leading at Scale)

Primary-source method note, not a book. The cluster already holds the assertion that mechanisms beat intentions (canon bezos shareholder letters) and a goal-setting tool (canon doerr measure what matters). Neither tells you how to build one. This note is the construction method, taken from the only place AWS publishes it in full.

  • Source: AWS Well-Architected, Building mechanisms + The ORR mechanism (tool / adoption / inspection / iteration / Appendix A) · AWS Enterprise Strategy, Strategy is a winding road; mechanisms keep you on track · AWS Prescriptive Guidance, Theme 8: Implement mechanisms for manual processes · Elements of Amazon's Day 1 Culture (Daniel Slater, AWS, 2023) · Amazon Science, How mechanism design theory helps optimize Amazon vendor collaboration

  • Core claim: A mechanism is not a process or a policy. Verbatim: "A mechanism is a complete process where you create a tool, drive adoption of the tool, and inspect the results in order to make course corrections… It takes controllable inputs and transforms them into ongoing outputs to address a recurring business challenge." Drop any one of the three legs and what you have is a good intention with paperwork.

  • Framework — the seven steps, as AWS actually built the ORR: 1. Work backwards from the challenge and state the outputs as countable results. AWS wanted availability, so it named three: incidents that are fewer, shorter, smaller. Not a vision statement — three things you can count, or you cannot inspect later. 2. Name the controllable inputs. For the ORR, "the design and operations of those services are the inputs." Skipping this step is the usual reason a mechanism never moves anything. 3. Build the smallest tool. The ORR's tool is a checklist of questions — each one a question, a paragraph of guidance, and answers carrying a risk rating ("Do any of your hosts pin certificates?" → ☐ Yes | High Risk, ☐ No | No Risk). The web service came years later. 4. Source the content from your own failures. Appendix A walks a real incident (a manual IAM change never written back into the CloudFormation template) into one checklist question. A mature mechanism is a compiled history of your own outages. 5. Get adoption by embedding in a lifecycle that already exists. Despite the name, the ORR is not a pre-launch gate — it is "built into the entire Software Development Lifecycle." New gates get routed around. 6. Inspect at three altitudes. Cadence: a weekly ops metrics meeting up to SVP level, where one inspected number is when a team last ran an ORR and how many action items are open. Per instance: a written narrative reviewed with leadership; high-criticality findings escalate into a go / no-go. Meta: the correction-of-error template asks "When was your last ORR performed?" and "Would any ORR recommendations have reduced or avoided the impact of this event?" — every failure audits the mechanism meant to prevent it. 7. Iterate, with a standing owner. "It's unlikely that a mechanism will operate as designed from day one." A specialist community ("Operational Champions") both challenges answers during reviews and curates the question list — checking each question asks the right thing and that its result can be measured.

  • Second framework — mechanism vs. guardrail: a guardrail is a wall that engages only in an emergency; a mechanism is a slope that re-centres you continuously. The image is a train wheel: the flange touches the rail only in a crisis, while the sloped tread quietly re-centres the train on every rotation. Design the slope. The cleanest example is a cloud migration run with no deadline: remaining on-premises costs were allocated across whatever applications stayed, so each team's bill rose as its neighbours left. Nobody was ordered to migrate; migrating became cheaper.

  • Third framework — when incentives are in play (Amazon Science): if the mechanism spans parties with private information, you need incentive compatibility — truthful reporting must be each party's best strategy "regardless of what the other side does" — and information privacy: the vendor "never reveals its cost structure, only its responses to iterative queries." The transferable moves are: price the deviation and charge it to whoever causes it; iterate proposals instead of demanding disclosure; offer a menu, not a mandate.

  • Applies when: the problem recurs, you have a countable output, and the behaviour you want currently depends on someone remembering. Also the diagnostic use: given anything called a process, name its tool, its adoption route, and its inspection — the missing leg is the answer.

  • Breaks when:

  • The problem is one-off. A mechanism on a non-recurring problem is pure overhead; that is a project. AWS is explicit that the cyclic form "is best suited for solving recurring problems."
  • Inspection has no gravity. The guide's own warning: "you will need to create an inspection process that has the gravity to drive both cultural change and adoption of the mechanism's tool." Without a forum senior people already attend, steps 1–5 decay into paperwork. Theme 8 makes the same point from the other side, naming executive sponsorship and named owners as prerequisites.
  • The process becomes the thing. Bezos, 2016: "You stop looking at outcomes and just make sure you're doing the process right… do we own the process or does the process own us?" This is the mechanism's own Day-2 failure, and the meta-inspection question in step 6 is the only defence in the material.
  • Aggregate reporting hides the tail. The Day 1 whitepaper: average growth "may mask underlying trends and drivers that affect a meaningful number of customers." A single contradicting anecdote is data about the tail. Pairs with canon tufte visual display and canon kahneman thinking fast and slow on what a summary statistic destroys.

  • The metric is self-reported by someone it judges. Then you have built a machine that rewards misreporting — see the incentive-compatibility framework above.

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (not yet mined from the Reddit / YouTube corpus — run python3 _ingest/pull.py before claiming an outside practitioner read.) Two counterpoints are available honestly without it. First, the mined corpus already in canon bezos shareholder letters shows the dissent mechanism is the one that reliably rots: r/ExperiencedDevs "I'm giving up; becoming a yes man" (1,668↑) and r/managers "the 'silent resignation' nobody notices" (9,401↑) document Day-2 stasis arriving not from bad mechanisms but from misaligned rewards underneath good ones. Second, and more usefully, this repository is itself a failed-mechanism case study: acumen/ shipped a complete tool on 2026-06-06 — six-dimension rubric, red-team protocol, memo spec, pass thresholds — and produced zero scored reps in sixteen weeks, because nothing cost anything when a week was skipped. learn/VALIDATION.md, which has all three legs, produced five documented turns of improvement in the same period. Same author, same repo; the difference is adoption and inspection. Written up in acumen/MECHANISM.md.

  • Shelf gap (deliberate, do not fake it): Bryar & Carr's Working Backwards is the book-length treatment of this material and the source of the PR/FAQ mechanism. It is cited inside canon bezos shareholder letters but has no note of its own. It should get one — from an actual read, not from summaries.

Rep

Take one thing you call a process. Write down its tool, who actually adopts it, and who inspects the result — with a date for the last inspection. Whichever of the three you cannot fill in is why it isn't working. Then add the meta-question to whatever template records your failures: would this mechanism have prevented the last one?

Marks itself read when you reach the end.
